title: The Research Brief: What's New in Learning Science
author: Carl Hendrick
summary: December learning science research shows retrieval practice boosts both memory and transfer to novel situations, problem solving before instruction strengthens conceptual understanding, and AI-generated summaries weaken learning compared to effortful information synthesis. Research also reveals fine motor skills correlate strongly with academic outcomes, explicit morphological instruction improves spelling, and autonomous learning without proper structure harms achievement. Teacher burnout stems from workload, insufficient support, and lack of autonomy rather than low pay alone. Students need structured guidance, meaningful retrieval opportunities, and classrooms emphasizing mastery over performance.
points: Three rounds of retrieval practice produce significantly better memory and transfer to novel applications than restudy, but benefits require multiple retrievals and consolidation time.
Problem solving before instruction strengthens conceptual understanding despite higher cognitive load, while direct instruction first helps procedural fluency and student preference.
Learners using AI-generated summaries understand less, produce weaker work, and spend less time engaging with sources than those who search and synthesize information themselves.
Fine motor skills correlate with academic outcomes as strongly as factors schools debate extensively, with connections running through both cognitive and direct pathways.
Teachers leave the profession primarily because of unsustainable workloads, poor administrative support, limited autonomy, and inadequate pay, not any single factor alone.
quotes: Three rounds of retrieval practice enhanced not just memorization but transfer to novel application questions one week later, outperforming both restudy and studying quiz questions with answers provided.
Problem solving before instruction led to slightly better conceptual learning and higher cognitive load, while instruction before problem solving supported procedural performance.
Learners who relied on AI-generated summaries understood less and produced weaker, less original work than those who searched and synthesised information themselves.
Fine motor skills and academic outcomes are linked about as strongly as many of the factors schools spend years debating.
Pupils do not automatically benefit from self directed approaches and many appear to need more explicit guidance than fashionable discourse suggests.

Teachers leave the profession primarily because of unsustainable workloads, poor administrative support, limited autonomy, and inadequate pay, leading to burnout and moral demoralization.” Archived from The Learning Dispatch on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
